title: Being Online
source_note: Written 2026-08-30 to explain the mechanics of feeds, ads, in-game purchases, scams and online safety to kids directly, rather than treating them as risks to be managed. Avoids naming specific platforms so the facts do not date.

questions.prompt: What is the main reason a video app or social media feed decides what to show you next?
choices: To keep you watching or scrolling for as long as possible
To show posts in the exact order they were uploaded
To only show what your friends have already seen
To save the company money on servers
questions.explanation: Feeds are built to hold your attention, because the longer you stay, the more adverts the app or site can show you.

questions.prompt: A video finishes and another one starts playing straight away, without you pressing anything. What is this feature usually called?
choices: Autoplay
A software error
A setting no app is able to turn off
Buffering
questions.explanation: Autoplay is a deliberate design choice. It removes the natural moment where you would normally decide whether to keep watching.

questions.prompt: In the phrase 'this app is designed for engagement', what does engagement mean?
choices: How much you click, watch, scroll and react
How much the app costs to download
How many bugs the app has
How fast the app opens
questions.explanation: Engagement is a measure of your attention and activity. Many apps are designed around growing it.

questions.prompt: What is a loot box in a video game?
choices: A random pack of in-game items you pay for without knowing exactly what you'll get
A box that stores your saved games
A free daily login gift with no cost
A tutorial level for new players
questions.explanation: You hand over money or in-game currency before you know what's inside, which is what makes loot boxes controversial.

questions.prompt: What is phishing?
choices: A message or website designed to trick you into handing over personal information
A type of virus that damages computer hardware
A setting that blocks spam phone calls
A game about catching virtual fish
questions.explanation: Phishing messages are built to look trustworthy so you will click a link or type in details like a password.

questions.prompt: Why is a password like 'password123' considered weak?
choices: It's short, common, and easy for a computer program to guess
It has too many characters
It only works on one website
It's too difficult for people to remember
questions.explanation: Programs used to crack passwords try common words and patterns first, so obvious passwords fall quickly.

questions.prompt: Which of these best describes a strong password?
choices: Long, and not an obvious word or pattern someone could guess
Exactly six letters long
Your own name spelled backwards
The same password you use for every account, so you never forget it
questions.explanation: Length and unpredictability are what make a password hard to crack, not how memorable it feels to you.

questions.prompt: What is a cookie, in the internet sense?
choices: A small file a website saves on your device to remember details about your visit
A type of computer virus
A snack you can order through a delivery app
A backup copy of your photos
questions.explanation: Cookies let a site remember things like whether you are logged in, but they can also be used to track you across the web.

questions.prompt: What is a 'digital footprint'?
choices: The trail of information left behind by what you post, search and click online
A setting on a phone's camera
A password used for online banking
A type of computer virus
questions.explanation: Every post, search and click can add to a picture of you that exists even after you have moved on.

questions.prompt: If a message online makes you feel scared, upset or unsafe, what is the best first step?
choices: Tell a trusted adult about it
Reply and argue back
Delete the app and never mention it to anyone
Ignore it and hope it stops on its own
questions.explanation: Telling a trusted adult is the sensible first move, even if it feels awkward. Adults can help, often more easily than it seems.

questions.prompt: Most feeds and video apps never really reach an 'end', unlike the last page of a book. Why?
choices: Infinite scroll is designed so there is no natural point to stop
The apps run out of storage space eventually
Old posts get deleted automatically after a while
Only some devices can show more than one page
questions.explanation: Removing a natural stopping point is deliberate. Without one, it is easier to keep scrolling past the point you meant to stop.

questions.prompt: A social media app is free to use. How does the company that runs it usually make money?
choices: By selling advertising space in people's feeds
By charging a small fee every time the app is opened
Through government funding
By selling the app itself in shops
questions.explanation: Attention is what is actually being sold. Advertisers pay to reach the people using the app.

questions.prompt: Which of these is most likely to be an advert, even if it appears among ordinary posts?
choices: A post labelled 'sponsored' or 'paid partnership'
A post from a friend about their weekend
A post with no pictures in it
A post written entirely in capital letters
questions.explanation: Labels like 'sponsored' or 'paid partnership' are the clearest sign a post is an advert, even when it is mixed in with normal content.

questions.prompt: A creator posts a video saying 'thanks to this brand for sending me this product to try'. What is this an example of?
choices: Sponsored content
A public service announcement
A software update notice
An independent news report
questions.explanation: When a creator is paid or given free products to feature something, it is sponsored content, even if it is presented casually.

questions.prompt: Loot boxes and similar in-game purchases are often designed with bright lights, music and a slow reveal. Why?
choices: To make opening one feel exciting, so you are more likely to want another
To help you understand the game's rules better
Because it's required by the device's operating system
To make the game load faster
questions.explanation: The build-up is deliberate. It is designed to make the moment feel rewarding, which encourages more spending.

questions.prompt: A message says 'Your account will be deleted, click here right now to stop it!' What detail should make you suspicious?
choices: The pressure to act immediately
The fact that it mentions an account at all
The use of the word 'click'
The length of the message
questions.explanation: Urgency is one of the biggest warning signs of a scam. Real companies rarely demand you act within minutes.

questions.prompt: You get a message saying you've won a prize in a competition you never entered. What is most likely going on?
choices: It's a scam trying to get your details or money
You genuinely won and should claim it straight away
It's an automatic message from your school
It's just a normal advert
questions.explanation: A prize for a competition you never entered is one of the oldest scam tricks there is.

questions.prompt: Why is using the same password on every account risky?
choices: If one site is hacked, that password can be used to get into your other accounts too
It makes your accounts run slower
Websites can tell you're reusing it and will delete your account
It uses more of your data allowance
questions.explanation: A leaked password from one site becomes a key that fits every other lock you used it on.

questions.prompt: What does a password manager do?
choices: Creates and remembers strong, different passwords for each of your accounts
Deletes your old passwords automatically
Shares your passwords with people you follow
Only works for one website at a time
questions.explanation: It takes away the need to remember dozens of passwords, so each one can be long and different.

questions.prompt: What is two-factor authentication (2FA)?
choices: A second check, like a code sent to your phone, needed alongside your password to log in
A password that must be exactly two words long
A rule requiring you to log in twice every day
A setting that makes your internet connection faster
questions.explanation: 2FA adds a second proof that it's really you, on top of the password.

questions.prompt: You look at shoes on one website, then start seeing shoe adverts on a completely different site. Why?
choices: Trackers can share information about what you viewed with advertising networks
The two websites are owned by your internet provider
It's simply a coincidence that happens to everyone
Your device broadcasts your browsing out loud
questions.explanation: Trackers built into many websites pass on details about what you viewed, which is how adverts seem to follow you around.

questions.prompt: Is asking a trusted adult for help with something that happened online ever a sign that you've failed?
choices: No, it's a sensible and completely normal thing to do
Yes, it means you can't cope online
Only if you're younger than ten
Only if it's happened to you more than once
questions.explanation: Asking for help is what capable people do. It solves the problem faster than struggling with it alone.

questions.prompt: Before sending a message online, which question is genuinely worth asking yourself first?
choices: Would I be comfortable saying this to the person's face?
Will this message load quickly for the other person?
Is this message under one hundred characters?
Will this get me the most likes or replies?
questions.explanation: If you wouldn't say it face to face, that's usually a sign to rewrite it or not send it at all.

questions.prompt: What is 'ad inventory'?
choices: The number of advert slots an app or website has available to sell
A list of every advert a person has ever clicked
The apps installed on someone's phone
A rule limiting how many adverts a person can see per day
questions.explanation: Every scroll, video break or search results page is a potential slot a company can sell to advertisers. That's its inventory.

questions.prompt: Why can adverts be hard to spot inside a feed, even when you're looking out for them?
choices: They are designed to look and feel like the ordinary posts around them
They are always the brightest colour on the screen
They are always placed at the very top of the page
They always contain the word 'advert' somewhere
questions.explanation: Blending in is the point. An advert that looks like a normal post is more likely to be watched or clicked.

questions.prompt: A game keeps offering small in-game purchases, each one only a couple of dollars. What is the real risk?
choices: Small amounts add up to a lot of real money over time, without feeling like it
The purchases always get automatically refunded after a week
Small purchases make the game run noticeably faster
Each purchase unlocks the entire game for free afterwards
questions.explanation: Small, frequent spending is easy to lose track of. It's the accumulated total that matters, not any single purchase.

questions.prompt: Scam messages often pretend to be from a bank, a well-known company or someone you know. Why?
choices: You're more likely to lower your guard with a name you already trust
It's the only way to legally send a message
Trusted names are the only ones free to use
It makes the message load faster
questions.explanation: Borrowing a trusted name is a shortcut past your suspicion, which is exactly why scammers do it.

questions.prompt: A fake website looks almost, but not quite, identical to a real one, and asks you to type in your password. What is this called?
choices: A phishing page
A firewall
A cache
A backup server
questions.explanation: Copying a real site's look, down to small details, is a common phishing trick used to steal login details.

questions.prompt: If you're worried about forgetting a new password, what is the safest place to keep a note of it?
choices: In a password manager, or somewhere private that others can't see
Taped to your computer screen
Posted in a group chat as a reminder
In your public profile bio
questions.explanation: A note anyone can see defeats the purpose of having a password at all.

questions.prompt: Why does 2FA still protect your account even if someone else learns your password?
choices: They would also need your phone or another device to get the extra code
It automatically changes your password every hour
It deletes the account after one wrong login attempt
It hides your account from search results
questions.explanation: The password alone isn't enough with 2FA switched on. Whoever's trying to log in also needs the second code.

questions.prompt: What is a 'tracker' doing when it's built into a webpage?
choices: Recording details about your visit, like which pages you viewed and for how long
Speeding up how quickly the page loads
Checking the page's text for spelling mistakes
Blocking adverts from appearing on the page
questions.explanation: Trackers quietly log behaviour, often to be used for advertising or to build a profile of visitors.

questions.prompt: Why do many websites now ask you to 'accept cookies' before you can use them?
choices: Laws in many countries require sites to ask permission before tracking visitors
It's only there to make the site look official
It stops the website from crashing
It's required to connect the device to WiFi
questions.explanation: Privacy laws in many places require websites to get some form of consent before using tracking cookies.

questions.prompt: Many popular apps and websites cost nothing to use. How do they still make money?
choices: Many earn money from advertising built around data about their users
They are entirely funded by charities
They are all run as unpaid school projects
Free apps never actually make any money
questions.explanation: If you're not paying with money, your attention and data are often what is being turned into revenue instead.

questions.prompt: What do privacy settings on an app or account mainly let you control?
choices: Who can see your posts, profile and other information
How fast the app runs on your device
How many friends or followers you're allowed to have
Which language the app displays
questions.explanation: Privacy settings are about audience: who gets to see what you share, not how the app performs technically.

questions.prompt: Setting a profile to 'private' or 'friends only' mainly does what?
choices: Limits who can see what you post to people you've approved
Makes your posts disappear automatically after a day
Stops the app from working properly
Makes using the account free forever
questions.explanation: A private setting restricts your audience. It doesn't change how long posts last or what the app costs.

questions.prompt: A message you send privately to one person can still end up seen by others. How?
choices: The other person can screenshot, save or forward it on
Private messages automatically become public after a week
It's against the law for anyone to ever share a private message
Private messages can't actually be saved by the receiver
questions.explanation: Sending something privately controls who you sent it to, not what the other person chooses to do with it afterwards.

questions.prompt: What is cyberbullying?
choices: Repeated unkind or threatening behaviour towards someone through messages, apps or online platforms
A game where players compete against each other online
A type of computer error message
Any single disagreement between two people online
questions.explanation: The key parts are that it's repeated and it's meant to upset or intimidate someone, not just one heated argument.

questions.prompt: Default privacy settings on a new account are often more open than most people would actually choose. What's a sensible response to that?
choices: Check and adjust the settings soon after signing up, rather than leaving them as they are
Assume the defaults already give the most privacy possible
Avoid using privacy settings at all, since they can't be changed later
Wait a year before checking any settings
questions.explanation: Companies often set defaults to share more, not less. A quick check after signing up is worth the few minutes it takes.

questions.prompt: You suddenly receive a 2FA code you didn't request. What does that most likely mean?
choices: Someone else has your password and is trying to log in
Your account has just been upgraded for free
The app is only checking that 2FA still works
It happens randomly and means nothing
questions.explanation: An unexpected code is a warning sign that someone else has your password. It's worth changing the password and telling a trusted adult.

questions.prompt: Some countries have looked at making rules around loot boxes in video games. What concern usually drives this?
choices: That loot boxes can work like a form of gambling for young players
That loot boxes use too much internet data
That loot boxes are always too easy to win
That loot boxes are only available in one language
questions.explanation: Paying for a random reward without knowing what you'll get shares features with gambling, which is why some governments have looked at regulating it.

questions.prompt: If you clear the cookies stored in your browser, what usually happens?
choices: Sites may forget your logins and preferences until you set them up again
Your device is instantly wiped completely
All your saved photos are deleted
The internet stops working on that device
questions.explanation: Cookies hold small bits of memory for a site, like being logged in. Clearing them just resets that memory, nothing more.

questions.prompt: A single post rarely reveals much on its own. Why can a company still build a detailed picture of someone over time?
choices: Lots of small pieces of information, added together over months or years, can reveal a great deal
Every post always contains a person's full home address
Companies are only allowed to look at one post per person, ever
It's technically impossible to combine information from different visits
questions.explanation: It's the accumulation that matters. Small details from many visits can add up to a surprisingly complete profile.

questions.prompt: Why do some employers or schools look up what's publicly visible about someone online?
choices: What's publicly visible can shape the impression others form of that person
It's the only way to confirm someone's name
It's a legal requirement for every online signup
Public posts are automatically deleted before anyone else can see them
questions.explanation: Whatever's public and searchable can be seen by people well beyond your friends, including people making decisions about you.

questions.prompt: If you see someone else being bullied online, what is a genuinely helpful response?
choices: Tell a trusted adult, and avoid sharing or forwarding it further
Share the messages as widely as possible so everyone can see
Publicly argue with the person doing the bullying
Do nothing, since it isn't your problem
questions.explanation: Forwarding it on spreads the harm further, even without meaning to. Telling an adult is the move that actually helps.

questions.prompt: Why might someone say things online that they would never say to a person's face?
choices: Not seeing the other person's reaction can make cruel words feel less real or serious
Online messages don't count as genuine communication
Screens make people naturally kinder
It's physically impossible to be unkind through text
questions.explanation: Distance and a lack of visible reaction can make it easier to say things a person would never say in person.

questions.prompt: Turning off 'personalised' or 'targeted' adverts in an app's settings usually does what?
choices: Changes which adverts you see, but doesn't stop adverts appearing altogether
Removes every advert from the app completely
Makes the app free if it wasn't already
Deletes all your data from the company's servers
questions.explanation: Turning off personalisation changes the targeting, not the business model. Adverts still pay for a free app.

questions.prompt: What is a 'dark pattern' in app or website design?
choices: A design trick that nudges you into doing something you might not otherwise choose, like staying subscribed
A colour scheme used for night mode
A bug that makes an app crash unexpectedly
A setting that blocks all notifications at once
questions.explanation: Examples include a hard-to-find cancel button or a box that's ticked by default: small design choices that steer your decisions without you quite noticing.

questions.prompt: A company shares data about its users with no names attached, calling it 'anonymised'. Why might someone still work out who a specific person is?
choices: Combining enough details, like age, suburb and interests, can narrow it down to one person
Anonymised data always has the person's name hidden in a separate file
It's completely impossible to link anonymised data back to a person
Anonymised data is automatically deleted within a day
questions.explanation: Research has repeatedly shown that a handful of details together, even with no name attached, can point to one specific person.

questions.prompt: You post a photo with no mention of where it was taken. How might people still work out the location?
choices: Photos can carry hidden location and time details, called metadata, unless it's removed
Photos always display the location in large visible text
It's impossible for a photo to reveal where it was taken
Only photos taken by professional cameras contain location details
questions.explanation: Many phones quietly save GPS coordinates and the time inside the photo file itself. Some apps strip this out automatically, others don't.

questions.prompt: A feed keeps showing you more of what you already click and watch. What can happen to the range of things you see, over time?
choices: It can quietly narrow, so you notice a smaller range of views and topics than you'd expect
It automatically balances out to show every possible viewpoint equally
It becomes completely random regardless of what you've watched
Nothing changes, since feeds show the same thing to everyone
questions.explanation: Showing more of what already holds your attention keeps you engaged, but it can slowly narrow the world a feed shows you.

questions.prompt: An app doesn't know your name, yet the adverts you see still feel oddly relevant to you. How is that possible?
choices: Adverts can be targeted using patterns like your device, location and browsing habits, not just a name
It's always pure coincidence with no targeting involved
Every advert shown is identical for every single user
Apps are required to ask for your name before showing any advert
questions.explanation: A name isn't needed to build a fairly accurate picture of someone's interests. Patterns of behaviour can be enough on their own.

questions.prompt: You see private messages that were shared without the sender's permission. What is the best thing to do?
choices: Avoid forwarding or sharing them further, and tell a trusted adult
Forward them on so more people are aware
Reply publicly to the messages
Save a copy for yourself in case it's needed later
questions.explanation: Forwarding shared-without-permission messages spreads the harm further. Telling an adult is what actually helps.
